10079.statement:
Each straight cut goes all the way across a round pizza. Given how many cuts are made, find the largest number of pieces the pizza can end up in.

## Input

One integer `N` per line, the number of cuts, with `0 ≤ N ≤ 210000000`. A negative number ends the input and is not processed.

## Output

For every `N`, print the maximum number of pieces on its own line, with no extra spaces.

## Notes

The answer for the largest `N` does not fit in a 32 bit integer.

11321.statement:
Sort a list of integers by a custom rule based on their remainder modulo `M`.

Order the numbers by `x mod M` from smallest to largest, where the remainder follows C rules: a negative number gives a remainder that is zero or negative, for example `-100 mod 3 = -1`. When two numbers have the same remainder:

- an odd number comes before an even number,
- two odd numbers go from larger to smaller,
- two even numbers go from smaller to larger.

## Input

Several test sets. Each starts with a line `N M` (`0 < N ≤ 10000`, `0 < M ≤ 10000`), followed by `N` lines with one 32 bit signed integer each. A line `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each set, print the line `N M`, then the `N` numbers in sorted order, one per line. Finish by printing the closing `0 0` as well.

706.statement:
Draw numbers the way a seven segment calculator display shows them, at a chosen size.

With size `s`, every digit is `s + 2` characters wide and `2s + 3` lines tall. Horizontal segments are `s` dashes `-`, vertical segments are `s` bars `|`, and every unused position is a space. Neighbouring digits are separated by exactly one column of spaces. Pad every digit to its full width, including the last one on a line.

## Input

Each line holds two integers `s n` with `1 ≤ s ≤ 10` and `0 ≤ n ≤ 99999999`. The line `0 0` ends the input and is not drawn.

## Output

For each line, draw `n` at size `s`, then print one empty line.

1203.statement:
A stream system runs several registered queries at the same time. A query with period `P` first reports `P` seconds after registration, then every `P` seconds after that. Find the first `K` reports in time order.

When several queries report at the same moment, the one with the smaller query number goes first.

## Input

First, up to 1000 lines of the form `Register Q P`, where `Q` is a unique query number and `P` its period, both between 1 and 3000. A line with `#` ends this part. The last line holds one integer `K` (`K ≤ 10000`).

## Output

Print the query numbers of the first `K` reports, one per line.

10405.title: Longest Common Subsequence
10405.statement:
Given two strings, find the length of their longest common subsequence: the longest sequence of characters that appears in both strings in the same order, not necessarily next to each other.

For example, `abcdgh` and `aedfhr` share `adh`, so the answer is 3.

## Input

Pairs of lines until the end of input. Each line of a pair is one string of at most 1000 characters.

## Output

For each pair, print the length of the longest common subsequence on its own line.

## Notes

Strings may contain any visible characters, and a line can be empty. Read whole lines rather than words.

bcacbcabbaccbab
bccabccbbabacbc

zz1yy2xx3ww4vv

aedfhr

abcdefghijklmnzyxwvutsrqpo
opqrstuvwxyzabcdefghijklmn

11806.statement:
Place exactly `K` cheerleaders on an `M × N` grid, at most one per cell, so that every one of the four border sides has at least one cheerleader on it. A corner cell counts for both sides it touches. Count how many different placements exist.

## Input

The first line is `T` (`T ≤ 50`). Each of the next `T` lines holds `M N K` with `2 ≤ M, N ≤ 20` and `K ≤ 500`.

## Output

For test case `i`, print `Case i: ` followed by the number of placements modulo `1000007`.

## Notes

The count can be very large, so only its remainder modulo `1000007` is printed.

1660.statement:
A network of `n` relays is joined by two way cables. Its safety factor is the smallest number of relays whose removal leaves the network disconnected. If no set of removals disconnects it, the safety factor is `n`. An empty network or a single relay counts as connected.

Compute the safety factor of each network.

## Input

Several data sets until the end of input. Each starts with `n m` (`0 ≤ n ≤ 50`), the number of relays and cables, followed by `m` pairs written as `(u,v)` with `0 ≤ u < v < n`. Apart from inside a pair, spacing and line breaks can appear anywhere.

## Output

For each data set, print its safety factor on its own line.

100.statement:
Start from a number `n` and repeat: if `n` is 1, stop; if it is odd, replace it by `3n + 1`; otherwise halve it. The cycle length of `n` is how many numbers appear in this sequence, counting `n` itself and the final 1. For example, 22 gives 16 numbers.

For each pair `i j`, find the largest cycle length among all numbers between `i` and `j`, inclusive.

## Input

Pairs of integers `i j`, one pair per line, until the end of input. Every number is between 1 and 9999.

## Output

For each pair, print `i`, `j` and the largest cycle length on one line, separated by spaces. Print `i` and `j` in the same order as in the input.

## Notes

`i` can be larger than `j`.

105.statement:
Rectangular buildings stand on a flat ground line. Building `k` is given as `(L, H, R)`: it spans from x = `L` to x = `R` and has height `H`. Describe the outline you see when all buildings are drawn together.

Write the outline as one sequence that alternates x coordinates and heights: start at the leftmost x, give the height that begins there, then the next x where the height changes, the new height, and so on. The sequence always ends with height 0.

## Input

Between 1 and 5000 lines, each with three integers `L H R` (`0 < L < R`, all below 10000). Lines are sorted by `L`.

## Output

One line with the outline sequence, numbers separated by single spaces.

108.statement:
Given an `N × N` grid of integers, find the rectangular block of adjacent cells (at least 1 × 1) with the largest total sum.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with `N` (`N ≤ 100`), followed by `N²` integers in row order, separated by any whitespace. Every value is between -127 and 127. `N = 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each test case, print the largest sum on its own line.

111.statement:
A history exam asks students to put `n` events in order. A student scores the length of the longest group of events they placed in the same relative order as the correct answer; the events in the group do not have to be next to each other.

Both the correct answer and each student answer are given as rankings: the `i`th number is the position assigned to event `i`, not the event placed at position `i`.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with `n` (`2 ≤ n ≤ 20`), then a line with the correct ranking, then any number of lines with student rankings. Every ranking is a permutation of 1 to `n`.

## Output

For each student ranking, print the score on its own line.

118.statement:
Robots move on a rectangular grid from `(0, 0)` to the given upper right corner. Each robot has a position and a facing (`N`, `E`, `S` or `W`) and follows a string of commands: `L` turns left, `R` turns right, `F` moves one step forward. North means `y` increases.

A robot that steps off the grid is lost, and it leaves a scent on the last cell it stood on. Later robots ignore any `F` command that would take them off the grid from a scented cell. Robots run one after another.

## Input

The first line gives the upper right corner. Then, for each robot, one line with `x y facing` and one line with its commands, until the end of input.

## Output

For each robot, print its final `x y facing`. If it was lost, print the last position before it fell off, followed by `LOST`.
118.sample_input:
5 3
1 1 E
RFRFRFRF
3 2 N
FRRFLLFFRRFLL
0 3 W
LLFFFLFLFL

122.statement:
Build binary trees from a list of nodes and print each one level by level.

Each node is written as `(v,path)`: value `v` (a positive integer) sits at the place reached from the root by following `path`, a string of `L` (left) and `R` (right). The root has an empty path, `(v,)`. A tree is listed as several nodes and ends with `()`.

A tree is complete only if every node on every path from the root has exactly one value.

## Input

Trees until the end of input. Nodes are separated by whitespace and a tree can span several lines. Each tree has between 1 and 256 nodes.

## Output

For each tree, print its values level by level, left to right within a level, separated by spaces. If the tree is not complete, print `not complete` instead.

141.statement:
Two players take turns on an `N × N` board. Each move either places a spot on an empty square or removes one. A player loses the moment they create a board pattern that has appeared before, either exactly or rotated by 90 or 180 degrees. If no pattern repeats in `2N` moves, the game is a draw.

## Input

Several games. Each starts with `N` (`2 ≤ N ≤ 50`), followed by `2N` moves, one per line, written as `row column +` or `row column -`. All `2N` moves are listed even if the game ends earlier. A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each game, print `Player p wins on move m` or `Draw`, where `p` is the winner and `m` the losing move.

160.statement:
Write `N!` by how many times each prime divides it, listed for every prime up to `N` in increasing order. For example `5! = 120` has three 2s, one 3 and one 5.

## Input

One integer `N` per line (`2 ≤ N ≤ 100`). A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each `N`, print `N` right aligned in 3 characters, then `! =`, then the prime counts, each right aligned in 3 characters. At most 15 counts go on one line; continuation lines are indented to line up under the first count. Match the sample output exactly.

165.statement:
A document may carry at most `h` stamps and there are `k` different stamp values. Choose the `k` values so that every amount from 1 up to some `n` can be paid with at most `h` stamps, and `n` is as large as possible. For example, with `h = 3, k = 2`, values 1 and 3 reach every amount up to 7, which is the best possible.

## Input

One pair `h k` per line, with `h + k ≤ 9`. The line `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each pair, print the largest possible `n` on its own line.

240.statement:
Build a Huffman code that uses the first `R` decimal digits as code symbols for the first `N` uppercase letters, given each letter's frequency.

In each step, take the `R` letters or groups with the lowest frequencies and merge them into one group; they receive digits 0 to `R - 1` in order of increasing frequency. Ties go to the group whose earliest letter comes first in the alphabet. If `N` does not allow every step to merge exactly `R` items, add extra letters of frequency 0 after the real ones first. A letter's code is the digits it received, read from the last merge back to the first.

## Input

Several data sets. Each line starts with `R` and `N`, followed by the `N` frequencies. A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For data set `k`, print `Set k; average length x` with the average code length (weighted by frequency) to two decimal places, then one line per real letter with the letter and its code, indented as in the sample. Print an empty line after each set. Follow the official statement for the exact layout.

242.statement:
An envelope holds at most `S` stamps. For a set of stamp values, its coverage is the largest amount `m` such that every amount from 1 to `m` can be paid with at most `S` stamps from that set.

For each data set, among several candidate sets pick the one with the largest coverage. Break ties by fewer values, then by the smaller largest value.

## Input

Several data sets. Each begins with `S` (`S ≤ 10`), then `N` (`N ≤ 10`), then `N` lines that each start with a count followed by that many increasing stamp values (at most 100). A data set with `S = 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each data set, print `max coverage =` followed by the coverage, a colon and the chosen values. The numbers are right aligned in fixed width fields; copy the spacing from the sample output.

255.statement:
A king and a queen stand on an 8 × 8 board whose squares are numbered 0 to 63, row by row. Pieces move only horizontally or vertically: the king one step, the queen any number of steps, and neither may pass through or land on the other piece. A move is allowed only if the destination is not a square the other piece could also move to.

Given the king's square, the queen's square and the square the queen moves to, judge the move.

## Input

One line per case with three integers from 0 to 63: king, queen, queen's new square. Input ends at the end of the file.

## Output

For each line print one of:

- `Illegal state` if king and queen share a square,
- `Illegal move` if the queen cannot legally reach the new square,
- `Move not allowed` if the king could also move to that square,
- `Stop` if after the move the king has no allowed move,
- `Continue` otherwise.
255.sample_output:
Illegal state
Illegal move
Illegal move
Illegal move
Move not allowed
Continue
Continue
Illegal move
Stop

263.statement:
Build a number chain from a starting number: sort its digits in descending order to get `a`, in ascending order to get `b`, and replace the number by `a - b`. Repeat until you produce a number that is already in the chain. The chain length is the count of distinct numbers produced.

## Input

Up to 5000 positive numbers below 10⁹, one per line. A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each number, print `Original number was n`, then one line `a - b = c` for every step, then `Chain length L`, then an empty line. Match the sample exactly.

264.statement:
List all fractions `p/q` in a grid where row `p` and column `q` hold `p/q`, and walk the grid diagonally in a zig zag: 1/1, 1/2, 2/1, 3/1, 2/2, 1/3, 1/4, 2/3, and so on. Find the term at a given position.

## Input

One integer per line, between 1 and 10⁷, until the end of input.

## Output

For each number `n`, print `TERM n IS p/q`.
264.sample_output:
TERM 3 IS 2/1
TERM 14 IS 2/4
TERM 7 IS 1/4

288.statement:
Evaluate an expression on very large non negative integers using `+`, `-`, `*` and `**` (power). Usual precedence applies: `**` first, then `*`, then `+` and `-` from left to right. There are no parentheses or spaces.

The base of a power is a single digit from 1 to 9 and the exponent is positive. Other numbers can have up to 1000 digits.

## Input

One expression per line, until the end of input, with at most 100 operators each.

## Output

For each expression, print its exact value on one line.

## Notes

Results can have thousands of digits and can be negative.

294.statement:
In the range from `L` to `U`, find the number with the most positive divisors. If several tie, take the smallest.

## Input

The first line is `N`. Each of the next `N` lines holds `L U` with `1 ≤ L ≤ U ≤ 10⁹` and `U - L ≤ 10000`.

## Output

For each range, print `Between L and U, P has a maximum of D divisors.` where `P` is the number found and `D` its divisor count.
294.sample_output:
Between 1 and 10, 6 has a maximum of 4 divisors.
Between 1000 and 1000, 1000 has a maximum of 16 divisors.
Between 999999900 and 1000000000, 999999924 has a maximum of 192 divisors.

297.statement:
A 32 × 32 black and white image is stored as a quadtree written in preorder: `p` is a node split into four quadrants (listed next, in a fixed order), `f` is an all black quadrant and `e` is an all white one.

Overlay two such images: a pixel is black if it is black in at least one of them. Count the black pixels in the result.

## Input

The first line is the number of test cases. Each case has two lines, each a quadtree string. Trees are at most 5 levels deep.

## Output

For each case, print `There are X black pixels.`
297.sample_input:

ppeeefpffeefe
pefepeefe
peeef
peefe
peeef
peepefefe
297.sample_output:
There are 640 black pixels.
There are 512 black pixels.
There are 384 black pixels.

299.statement:
A train's carriages are numbered 1 to `L` but stand in some order. One operation swaps two neighbouring carriages. Find the fewest swaps needed to put them in order 1, 2, ..., `L`.

## Input

The first line is the number of test cases. Each case has a line with `L` (`0 ≤ L ≤ 50`) and a line with a permutation of 1 to `L`.

## Output

For each case, print `Optimal train swapping takes S swaps.`
299.sample_output:
Optimal train swapping takes 1 swaps.
Optimal train swapping takes 6 swaps.
Optimal train swapping takes 1 swaps.

300.statement:
Convert dates from the Maya Haab calendar to the Tzolkin calendar.

**Haab:** a year has 19 months. The first 18 have 20 days numbered 0 to 19 and are named `pop, no, zip, zotz, tzec, xul, yoxkin, mol, chen, yax, zac, ceh, mac, kankin, muan, pax, koyab, cumhu`. The last month, `uayet`, has 5 days numbered 0 to 4. A date is written `day. month year`.

**Tzolkin:** each day has a number cycling 1 to 13 and a name cycling through `imix, ik, akbal, kan, chicchan, cimi, manik, lamat, muluk, ok, chuen, eb, ben, ix, mem, cib, caban, eznab, canac, ahau`, both advancing every day. A year is 260 days. A date is written `number name year`.

The first day of the world is `0. pop 0` in Haab and `1 imix 0` in Tzolkin.

## Input

The first line is `n`, followed by `n` Haab dates, one per line. Years are below 5000.

## Output

Print `n` on the first line, then the Tzolkin date for each input date, in order.

302.statement:
A town has junctions and two way streets, each street with a unique number. Find a round trip that uses every street exactly once and ends where it started. Among all such trips, print the one whose sequence of street numbers is smallest in lexicographic order.

The trip starts at the smaller of the two junctions of the first street listed in the input.

## Input

Several blocks. Each line of a block is `x y z`: street `z` connects junctions `x` and `y` (they may be equal). A line `0 0` ends a block, and an empty block `0 0` ends the input. Junctions are at most 44 and streets fewer than 1995.

For each block, print the street numbers of the trip separated by spaces, or `Round trip does not exist.`, followed by an empty line.

357.statement:
Count the different ways to make an amount of money with US coins of 1, 5, 10, 25 and 50 cents. Ways differ in how many coins of each value are used, not in order.

## Input

One amount per line, from 0 to 30000 cents, until the end of input.

## Output

For each amount `n` with `m` ways, print `There are m ways to produce n cents change.` When `m` is 1, print `There is only 1 way to produce n cents change.` instead.

## Notes

The number of ways does not fit in a 32 bit integer for large amounts.
357.sample_output:
There are 6 ways to produce 17 cents change.
There are 4 ways to produce 11 cents change.
There is only 1 way to produce 4 cents change.

378.statement:
Each case gives two lines in the plane, each through two distinct points. Decide whether the lines are parallel, the same line, or cross in one point, and give the point.

## Input

The first line is `N` (`1 ≤ N ≤ 10`). Each of the next `N` lines has eight integers `x1 y1 x2 y2 x3 y3 x4 y4`: the first line passes through the first two points, the second line through the last two. Values are between -1000 and 1000.

## Output

Print `INTERSECTING LINES OUTPUT`, then one line per case: `NONE` for parallel lines, `LINE` for the same line, or `POINT x y` with both coordinates to two decimal places. Finish with `END OF OUTPUT`.
378.sample_output:

NONE
LINE
POINT 2.00 5.00
POINT 1.07 2.20
END OF OUTPUT

380.statement:
Simulate call forwarding in an office phone system. A request `source time duration target` forwards calls for extension `source` to `target` from hour `time` to `time + duration`, inclusive. Forwarding can chain: if the target also forwards at that moment, follow it on. If the chain comes back to the extension that was originally called, the call goes to the dead end extension `9999`.

## Input

The first line is the number of systems (at most 10). Each system lists up to 100 requests as four digit numbers `source time duration target`, ended by a line whose source is `0000`. Then come calls `time extension` in non decreasing time order, ended by a line whose time is `9000`.

## Output

Print `CALL FORWARDING OUTPUT`. For system `k` print `SYSTEM k`, then for each call `AT time CALL TO extension RINGS final`, with all numbers as four digits. Finish with `END OF OUTPUT`.

382.statement:
Classify each number by the sum of its proper divisors (all positive divisors except the number itself): it is perfect if the sum equals the number, abundant if the sum is larger, and deficient if it is smaller. For example 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 is perfect.

## Input

Between 1 and 99 positive integers, each at most 60000, separated by whitespace. A `0` ends the list.

## Output

Print `PERFECTION OUTPUT`. For each number, print it right aligned in 5 characters, two spaces, then `PERFECT`, `DEFICIENT` or `ABUNDANT`. Finish with `END OF OUTPUT`.

   28  PERFECT
    6  PERFECT
   56  ABUNDANT
60000  ABUNDANT
   22  DEFICIENT
  496  PERFECT
END OF OUTPUT

389.statement:
Convert a number from one base to another. Bases go from 2 to 16 and use the digits `0` to `9` and `A` to `F`.

The result is shown on a 7 digit display: pad it with leading zeros to exactly 7 digits, and if it is longer than 7 digits keep only the rightmost 7.

## Input

One conversion per line until the end of input: the number (it may have leading zeros), the base it is in, and the base to convert to, separated by one or more spaces.

## Output

For each line, print the 7 digit result.

## Notes

This version always prints exactly 7 digits, which differs from the original UVa problem.

397.statement:
Solve a simple equation one operation at a time. The left side is an integer expression with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, and the right side is a variable name.

Perform `*` and `/` first, left to right, then `+` and `-`, left to right. After every single operation, print the whole equation again with that operation replaced by its result.

## Input

One equation per line until the end of input, with 1 to 20 operations. Numbers can carry a sign such as `-3` or `+4`. Spaces are optional anywhere. Variable names have 1 to 8 letters. Every division is exact.

## Output

For each equation, print the original equation and then one line per step, ending with `value = variable`. Separate equations with an empty line. Spacing inside a line is not important, but write negative numbers like `-6` and positive ones without a sign.

401.statement:
Classify each string as a palindrome, a mirrored string, both, or neither.

A palindrome reads the same backwards. A mirrored string becomes itself when every character is replaced by its mirror image and the result is read backwards. Mirror pairs: `A-A, E-3, H-H, I-I, J-L, M-M, O-O, S-2, T-T, U-U, V-V, W-W, X-X, Y-Y, Z-5, 1-1, 8-8`. Every other character has no mirror, so a string containing one cannot be mirrored. The digit `0` never appears; only the letter `O` does.

## Input

One string per line until the end of input, 1 to 20 valid characters each.

## Output

For each string print the string followed by one of `-- is not a palindrome.`, `-- is a regular palindrome.`, `-- is a mirrored string.` or `-- is a mirrored palindrome.`, then an empty line.
401.sample_output:
NOTAPALINDROME -- is not a palindrome.

ISAPALINILAPASI -- is a regular palindrome.

2A3MEAS -- is a mirrored string.

ATOYOTA -- is a mirrored palindrome.

406.statement:
List the primes from 1 to `N`; in this problem 1 counts as a prime. Print the middle part of that list: the `2C` middle primes if the list has an even length, or the `2C - 1` middle primes if it is odd. If that is more than the whole list, print the whole list.

## Input

One line per case with `N C` (`1 ≤ N ≤ 1000`, `1 ≤ C ≤ N`), until the end of input.

## Output

For each case print `N C:` followed by the chosen primes, each preceded by one space, then an empty line.

409.title: Excuses, Excuses!
409.statement:
Find the excuses that contain the most keywords. A keyword counts each time it appears as a whole word, ignoring upper or lower case. A whole word means it is surrounded by the start or end of the line or by characters that are not letters.

## Input

Several sets until the end of input. Each starts with `K E` (`1 ≤ K, E ≤ 20`), then `K` lines with one lowercase keyword each, then `E` lines with one excuse each (up to 70 characters of letters, digits, spaces and `".,!?`).

## Output

For set `k`, print `Excuse Set #k`, then every excuse with the highest count, exactly as given, one per line, then an empty line. If several excuses tie, print them in input order.

dog

I am actually crazy.
1234567890.....,,,,,0987654321?????!!!!!!

409.sample_output:

Excuse Set #2

437.statement:
You have `n` kinds of boxes, unlimited copies of each, with sides `x y z`. A box can be turned so that any side is the height. A box can sit on another only if both sides of its base are strictly smaller than the two base sides of the box below. Find the tallest possible tower.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with `n` (`n ≤ 30`), then `n` lines with three integers each. `n = 0` ends the input.

## Output

For test case `k`, print `Case k: maximum height = h`.

Case 1: maximum height = 40
Case 2: maximum height = 21
Case 3: maximum height = 28
Case 4: maximum height = 342

439.statement:
Find the fewest knight moves between two squares of a standard 8 × 8 chessboard.

## Input

One case per line until the end of input: two squares separated by a space, each written as a column letter `a` to `h` and a row digit `1` to `8`.

## Output

For each case, print `To get from xx to yy takes n knight moves.`

To get from b1 to c3 takes 1 knight moves.

441.statement:
Given a set `S` of `k` numbers, print every way to choose 6 of them.

## Input

One case per line: `k` (`6 < k < 13`) followed by the `k` numbers of `S` in increasing order. A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

Print each choice on its own line, its numbers increasing and separated by single spaces, with all choices in lexicographic order. Separate test cases by one empty line, with no empty line after the last one.

455.statement:
A string has period `k` if it is made of one piece of length `k` repeated one or more times. For example `abcabcabcabc` has periods 3, 6 and 12. Find the smallest period of each string.

## Input

The first line is `N`, followed by an empty line. Then `N` strings of up to 80 non blank characters, with an empty line between consecutive strings.

## Output

For each string print its smallest period, with an empty line between consecutive answers.

458.statement:
Each line of the input is a message in which every character has been shifted by the same fixed amount in the ASCII table. Decode the messages. The example below the statement is enough to work out the shift.

## Input

Encoded lines until the end of input.

## Output

Print each decoded line.
458.sample_output:
*CDC is the trademark of the Control Data Corporation.
*IBM is a trademark of the International Business Machine Corporation.
*DEC is the trademark of the Digital Equipment Corporation.

482.statement:
Rearrange a list of numbers with an index array: if the index array is `p`, the `i`th input number moves to position `p[i]`.

## Input

The first line is the number of cases, then an empty line. Each case has two lines: a permutation of 1 to `n`, and `n` decimal numbers. Cases are separated by empty lines.

## Output

For each case, print the rearranged numbers one per line, each written exactly as it appeared in the input. Separate cases with an empty line.

483.statement:
Reverse the characters of every word while keeping the words in their original order. A word is any run of printable characters between whitespace, so punctuation is reversed with it.

## Input

Several lines of words until the end of input.

## Output

The same lines with each word reversed and spacing between words kept as in the input.

I love you.
You love me.
We're a happy family.

I evol .uoy
uoY evol .em
er'eW a yppah .ylimaf

488.statement:
Draw a triangle wave with a given amplitude, repeated a given number of times. One wave with amplitude `A` is the lines `1`, `22`, `333`, ... up to the digit `A` written `A` times, then back down to `1`.

## Input

The first line is the number of cases, followed by an empty line. Each case has two lines: the amplitude (at most 9) and the frequency, the number of waves. Cases are separated by empty lines.

## Output

For each case, print the waves with an empty line between consecutive waves, and an empty line between consecutive cases. Do not print extra empty lines after the last wave of the last case.

494.statement:
Count the words on each line, where a word is a maximal run of letters (`A` to `Z` or `a` to `z`). Any other character separates words.

## Input

Lines of text until the end of input.

## Output

For each line, print its word count.

Meep Meep!
I tot I taw a putty tat.
I did! I did! I did taw a putty tat.
Shsssssssssh ... I am hunting wabbits. Heh Heh Heh Heh ...

496.statement:
Compare two sets of distinct integers.

## Input

Pairs of lines until the end of input: the first line of a pair lists set A, the second set B.

## Output

For each pair print exactly one of:

- `A equals B`
- `A is a proper subset of B`
- `B is a proper subset of A`
- `A and B are disjoint`
- `I'm confused!` when none of the above holds.

## Notes

A set line can be empty.
496.sample_output:
A equals B
B is a proper subset of A
A is a proper subset of B
A and B are disjoint
I'm confused!

499.statement:
For each line of text, find the letters that occur most often. Uppercase and lowercase letters count separately, and characters that are not letters are ignored.

## Input

Lines of text until the end of input.

## Output

For each line, print all letters with the highest count, uppercase letters first in alphabetical order, then lowercase letters in alphabetical order, with no spaces between them. Then a space and the count.
499.sample_input:
When riding your bicycle backwards down a one-way street, if the
wheel falls of a canoe, how many ball bearings does it take to fill
up a water buffalo?
Hello Howard.

501.statement:
A black box starts empty with a counter `i = 0` and handles two operations: `ADD(x)` puts `x` in the box, and `GET` increases `i` by one and reports the `i`th smallest number currently in the box.

The operations are given as two lists: `A`, the numbers added in order, and `u`, where `u(p)` means the `p`th `GET` happens right after the first `u(p)` numbers have been added.

## Input

The first line is `K`, then an empty line, then `K` data sets separated by empty lines. Each data set holds `M N`, then `A(1..M)`, then `u(1..N)`, all separated by spaces or line breaks. `M, N ≤ 30000`, `|A| ≤ 2·10⁹`, `u` is non decreasing and `p ≤ u(p) ≤ M`.

## Output

For each data set, print the answer of each `GET` on its own line. Put an empty line between data sets.

512.statement:
Track where spreadsheet cells end up after a series of edits. Rows and columns are numbered from 1.

Operations:

- `EX r1 c1 r2 c2` swaps the contents of two cells.
- `DR A x1 ... xA` deletes the listed rows; `DC` does the same for columns.
- `IR A x1 ... xA` inserts an empty row before each listed row; `IC` does the same for columns.

All labels in one insert or delete command refer to the sheet before that command.

## Input

Several spreadsheets. Each starts with `rows columns` (at most 50 each), then the number of operations and the operations, then the number of queries and that many `r c` pairs about original cells. The line `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For spreadsheet `k`, print `Spreadsheet #k`, then for each query either `Cell data in (r,c) moved to (r2,c2)` or `Cell data in (r,c) GONE`. Put an empty line between spreadsheets.

Spreadsheet #1
Cell data in (4,8) moved to (4,6)
Cell data in (5,5) GONE
Cell data in (7,8) moved to (7,6)
Cell data in (6,5) moved to (1,2)

514.statement:
Coaches 1 to `N` arrive in that order and enter a dead end station that works like a stack: the last coach in is the first one out. Coaches leave toward the other side one at a time. Decide whether a given outgoing order is possible.

## Input

Several blocks. Each starts with `N` (`N ≤ 1000`), then one or more lines with a permutation of 1 to `N`, then a line with `0`. A block made only of `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each permutation print `Yes` or `No`. Print an empty line after each block.

516.statement:
A number is written by its prime factorisation: pairs `p e` meaning prime `p` raised to `e`, listed from the largest prime to the smallest. For each given number `x`, print `x - 1` in the same form.

## Input

One number per line, written as its prime factor pairs, where `2 < x ≤ 32767`. A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each line, print the factor pairs of `x - 1` from the largest prime to the smallest, all separated by single spaces.

534.statement:
A frog wants to get from stone 1 to stone 2 by jumping between stones. The difficulty of a route is its longest single jump. Find the smallest possible difficulty over all routes.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with `n` (`2 ≤ n ≤ 200`), then `n` lines with the integer coordinates of the stones (0 to 1000). An empty line follows each case. `n = 0` ends the input.

## Output

For test case `k`, print `Scenario #k`, then `Frog Distance = d` with `d` to three decimal places, then an empty line, also after the last case.
534.sample_output:
Scenario #1
Frog Distance = 5.000

Scenario #2
Frog Distance = 1.414

536.statement:
A binary tree has a different uppercase letter in every node. Given its preorder traversal (root, left, right) and its inorder traversal (left, root, right), print its postorder traversal (left, right, root).

## Input

One case per line until the end of input: the preorder string and the inorder string, separated by a space.

## Output

For each case, print the postorder string.

540.statement:
Simulate a team queue. Every element belongs to a team. A new element walks along the queue and stands right behind the last member of its team already waiting; if none is waiting, it joins at the back. Elements leave from the front as usual.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with the number of teams `t` (`t ≤ 1000`), then one line per team: its size followed by its elements (integers up to 999999). Then commands: `ENQUEUE x`, `DEQUEUE` and `STOP`, which ends the case. `t = 0` ends the input.

## Output

For test case `k`, print `Scenario #k`, then each element removed by `DEQUEUE` on its own line, then an empty line, also after the last case.

## Notes

A test case can have up to 200000 commands.

541.statement:
A 0/1 matrix has the parity property when every row and every column contains an even number of 1s. Check a matrix: is it fine already, can it be fixed by flipping exactly one bit, or is it corrupt?

## Input

Several matrices. Each starts with `n` (`n < 100`), followed by `n` lines of `n` values, each 0 or 1. `n = 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each matrix print `OK`, or `Change bit (i,j)` with the 1 based row `i` and column `j` to flip, or `Corrupt`.

543.statement:
Write each even number `n` as the sum of two odd primes `a + b`. If there are several ways, choose the one where `b - a` is largest.

## Input

Even integers `n` with `6 ≤ n < 1000000`, one per line. A `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each `n` print `n = a + b` with single spaces around `=` and `+`. If no pair exists, print `Goldbach's conjecture is wrong.`

544.statement:
Roads between cities each have a weight limit. A truck's load must not exceed the limit of any road it drives on. Find the heaviest load that can be carried from the start city to the destination.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with `n r` (`2 ≤ n ≤ 200` cities, `1 ≤ r ≤ 19900` roads), then `r` lines `cityA cityB limit` (two way roads, limits 0 to 10000), then a line with the start and destination names. Names have at most 30 characters and no spaces. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For test case `k`, print `Scenario #k`, then `y tons` with the maximum load, then an empty line.

579.statement:
Find the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of an analog clock at a given time. The hour hand moves smoothly as the minutes pass.

## Input

One time per line in the form `H:MM` with `1 ≤ H ≤ 12` and `00 ≤ MM ≤ 59`. The line `0:00` ends the input.

## Output

For each time, print the angle in degrees, between 0 and 180, with three digits after the decimal point.

591.statement:
Stacks of bricks have different heights. Move bricks one at a time so that every stack ends up the same height, using as few moves as possible. The total always divides evenly.

## Input

Several sets. Each has a line with `n` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 50`) and a line with the `n` heights (1 to 100). `n = 0` ends the input.

## Output

For set `k`, print `Set #k`, then `The minimum number of moves is m.`, then an empty line.
591.sample_output:
Set #1
The minimum number of moves is 5.

612.statement:
The unsortedness of a string is the number of pairs of positions `i < j` whose letters are in the wrong order (`s[i] > s[j]`). Sort DNA strings from least to most unsorted.

## Input

The first line is `M`, then an empty line, then `M` data sets separated by empty lines. Each data set starts with `n m` (`n ≤ 50` is the length, `m ≤ 100` the count), followed by `m` strings of length `n` using only `A`, `C`, `G`, `T`.

## Output

For each data set, print the strings from least to most unsorted. Strings with the same value keep their input order. Put an empty line between data sets.

ATCGATGCAT
TTTTGGCCAA
TTTGGCCAAA

615.statement:
Decide whether a set of directed edges forms a tree: exactly one node (the root) has no edge pointing to it, every other node has exactly one edge pointing to it, and every node can be reached from the root.

## Input

Several test cases. Each is a list of pairs `a b` (an edge from `a` to `b`, node numbers 1 to 100), spread over any number of lines and ended by `0 0`. The pair `-1 -1` ends the input.

## Output

For test case `k`, print `Case k is a tree. Root is r.` or `Case k is not a tree.`
615.sample_output:
Case 1 is a tree. Root is 5.
Case 2 is a tree. Root is 7.
Case 3 is not a tree.

630.statement:
Two words are anagrams if one is a rearrangement of the letters of the other. For each test word, list every word in the vocabulary that is an anagram of it, including the word itself if it is in the vocabulary.

## Input

The first line is `T`, then an empty line, then `T` test cases separated by empty lines. Each case has `N` (`N < 1000`), then `N` vocabulary words, then test words one per line, ended by `END`. Words are lowercase with at most 20 letters.

## Output

For each test word, print `Anagrams for: word`, then the matching vocabulary words in vocabulary order, each as `k) word` with `k` right aligned in 3 characters. If there are none, print `No anagrams for: word` instead. Put an empty line between test cases.

  1) microphotographics

657.statement:
A picture shows dice: `.` is background, `*` is part of a die and `X` is part of a dot on a die. Pixels belong together only if they share a side. A die is a group of connected `*` and `X` pixels; a dot is a group of connected `X` pixels. Count the dots on every die.

## Input

Several pictures. Each starts with `w h` (`5 ≤ w, h ≤ 50`), followed by `h` lines of `w` characters. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For picture `k`, print `Throw k`, then the dot counts of all dice in increasing order on one line, separated by spaces, then an empty line.

665.statement:
Among `N` coins exactly one is fake: it is either lighter or heavier than the others, which all weigh the same. Given the results of several weighings on a balance, find the fake coin if the results identify it uniquely.

## Input

The first line is `M`, then an empty line, then `M` data sets separated by empty lines. Each starts with `N K` (`N, K ≤ 100`). Each of the `K` weighings takes two lines: `P` followed by `P` coins on the left pan and `P` coins on the right pan; then `<`, `>` or `=` for the result.

## Output

For each data set, print the fake coin's number, or `0` if it cannot be determined. Put an empty line between data sets.

673.statement:
A string of `(`, `)`, `[` and `]` is correct if it is empty, or two correct strings joined together, or a correct string wrapped in `( )` or `[ ]`. Check each string.

## Input

The first line is `n`, followed by `n` strings, one per line, each up to 128 characters.

## Output

For each string print `Yes` or `No`.

## Notes

A line can be empty, and the empty string is correct.

674.statement:
Count the different ways to make an amount using coins of 1, 5, 10, 25 and 50 cents. Ways differ in how many coins of each value are used. There is exactly one way to make 0 cents.

## Input

One amount per line, at most 7489 cents, until the end of input.

## Output

For each amount, print the number of ways on its own line.

679.statement:
A full binary tree of depth `D` has nodes numbered level by level, left to right, starting with 1 at the root. Every inner node has a switch that starts pointing left. A ball dropped from the root goes down until it reaches a leaf; at each inner node it flips the switch and goes the way the switch pointed before the flip. Balls are dropped one after another. Find the leaf where ball number `I` stops.

## Input

The first line is the number of test cases. Each next line holds `D I` with `2 ≤ D ≤ 20` and `1 ≤ I ≤ 524288`, never more than the number of leaves. A line with `-1` ends the input.

## Output

For each test case, print the number of the leaf.

686.statement:
Count the ways to write an even number `n` as the sum of two primes `p1 + p2`. A pair and its reverse count once.

## Input

One even number per line with `4 ≤ n < 32768`. A `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each number, print the count on its own line.

696.statement:
Find the largest number of knights that can be placed on an `M × N` chessboard so that no knight attacks another. A knight attacks squares two rows and one column away, or one row and two columns away.

## Input

Pairs `M N` (each at most 500), one per line. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each pair print `k knights may be placed on a M row N column board.`
696.sample_output:
4 knights may be placed on a 2 row 3 column board.
13 knights may be placed on a 5 row 5 column board.
14 knights may be placed on a 4 row 7 column board.

709.statement:
Rewrap each paragraph so that every line is exactly `n` characters wide, including the last one. Words stay in order and are never split; lines start and end with a word.

Every gap of `g` spaces between two words costs `(g - 1)²`. A line with a single word is left aligned, and costs 500 if it is shorter than `n`. Choose the layout with the smallest total cost. If several layouts tie, compare them gap by gap from the start and prefer the one whose first differing gap is smaller.

## Input

Several paragraphs. Each starts with a line holding `n` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 80`), then one or more lines of words separated by spaces, then one empty line. Words use characters with codes 33 to 126 and are never longer than `n`. A paragraph with `n = 0` ends the input.

## Output

Print each formatted paragraph followed by an empty line.
709.sample_input:
28
This is the example you are
actually considering.

25
Writing e-mails is fun, and with this program,
they even look nice.

0
709.sample_output:
This  is  the  example   you
are  actually   considering.

Writing e-mails  is  fun,
and  with  this  program,
they  even   look   nice.

714.statement:
Split a row of `m` books into `k` consecutive groups, each with at least one book, so that the largest total number of pages in a group is as small as possible. Among all best splits, give the first group as little as possible, then the second, and so on.

## Input

The first line is the number of cases. Each case has a line `m k` (`1 ≤ k ≤ m ≤ 500`) and a line with the `m` page counts, each below 10⁷.

## Output

For each case, print the page counts in order with ` / ` between groups: one space between numbers and one space on each side of every slash.

## Notes

Sums can exceed a 32 bit integer.

725.statement:
Find every pair of five digit numbers `abcde / fghij = N` such that the ten digits are all different, so 0 to 9 each appear once. Either number may start with 0.

## Input

One integer `N` per line with `2 ≤ N ≤ 79`. A `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each `N`, print every solution as `abcde / fghij = N` in increasing order of the first number, writing both numbers with five digits. If there are none, print `There are no solutions for N.` Put an empty line between the outputs of different `N`.

748.statement:
Compute `R` to the power `n` exactly, where `R` is a decimal number with `0.0 < R < 99.999` and `n` is an integer with `0 < n ≤ 25`.

## Input

One pair per line until the end of input: `R` in the first six columns, then `n`.

## Output

For each pair, print the exact value of `R` to the power `n`. Leave out leading zeros, including the zero before the decimal point for values below 1 (print `.0512`, not `0.0512`), and trailing zeros after the decimal point. If the value is a whole number, print it without a decimal point.

753.statement:
A room has one outlet of each listed type. Devices each need an outlet of a certain plug type. Adapters convert one plug type into another, can be chained, and are available in unlimited numbers, but each outlet still serves one device. Plug in as many devices as possible and report how many are left without power.

## Input

The first line is the number of cases, then an empty line. Each case lists `n` outlet types, then `m` devices as `name plugType`, then `k` adapter kinds as `outletType plugType` meaning the adapter offers `outletType` and plugs into `plugType`. Counts are at most 100 and names at most 24 characters. Cases are separated by empty lines.

## Output

For each case, print the smallest number of devices that cannot be plugged in. Put an empty line between cases.

798.title: Tile Puzzle
798.statement:
Rebuild a `w × h` rectangle using every tile from a collection. Tiles with the same size form a group and are indistinguishable from each other; tiles are placed without rotating. Count the different arrangements, where two arrangements differ if some group's tiles occupy different positions.

## Input

Data sets until the end of input. Each is `w h n` (`0 < w, h ≤ 100`, `0 < n ≤ 10`) followed by `n` groups `m wk hk`: `m` tiles of width `wk` and height `hk`. The tiles always fill the rectangle exactly.

## Output

For each data set, print the number of arrangements.

815.statement:
A region is a grid of 10 m × 10 m squares with given elevations. A given volume of water collects in the lowest squares first and spreads evenly, as if all squares were connected. Find the water level and the share of squares that end up strictly below it.

## Input

Several regions. Each starts with `m n` (both below 30), then `m` lines of `n` elevations in meters, then the water volume in cubic meters. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For region `k`, print `Region k`, then `Water level is x meters.`, then `y percent of the region is under water.`, both numbers to two decimal places, then an empty line.
815.sample_output:
Region 1
Water level is 46.67 meters.
66.67 percent of the region is under water.

820.statement:
A network has `n` nodes joined by two way connections, each with a bandwidth (the total in both directions). Find the largest total amount of data per time that can flow from node `s` to node `t`, splitting it over several paths if needed.

## Input

Several networks. Each starts with `n` (`2 ≤ n ≤ 100`), then `s t c`, then `c` lines `a b bandwidth` (bandwidth 0 to 1000). Two nodes can share several connections. A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For network `k`, print `Network k`, then `The bandwidth is x.`, then an empty line.

828.statement:
Decrypt messages made with this cipher. The key is a letter list `L` and a shift `N` (1 to 25). `ciph(p)` moves a letter `N` places forward in the alphabet, wrapping from `Z` to `A`.

Each word is encrypted from left to right. A letter not in `L` becomes `ciph(p)`. A letter in `L` becomes three letters: the `m`th letter of `L`, then `ciph(p)`, then the `(m+1)`th letter of `L`, after which `m` increases by one; `L` wraps around. `m` starts at 1 for every message and continues across its words. Spaces are kept.

## Input

The first line is the number of cases, then an empty line. Each case gives `L`, then `N`, then the number of messages, then one encrypted message per line. Cases are separated by empty lines.

## Output

For each message, print the original text, or `error in encryption` if it cannot be the result of this cipher. Put an empty line between cases.

RSAEIO
2
5
RTSSKAEAGE
GRSCAV
RGSSCAV
RUSIQO
RUSSGAACEV JEGIITOOGR

RICE
error in encryption
EAT
error in encryption
SEAT HERE

834.statement:
Write a fraction as a continued fraction `[b0; b1, b2, ..., bn]`, meaning `b0 + 1/(b1 + 1/(b2 + ... + 1/bn))`, where `b1` to `bn` are positive. To make the answer unique, the last term `bn` must be greater than 1 (unless the expansion has only `b0`). For example `43/19 = [2;3,1,4]`.

## Input

Pairs `numerator denominator` until the end of input.

## Output

For each pair, print the expansion as `[b0;b1,b2,...,bn]` with no spaces: a semicolon after the first term and commas between the others.

846.statement:
You walk along the number line from `x` to `y`. Each step's length is a non negative integer that is one more, the same, or one less than the previous step's length. The first and the last step must both have length 1. Find the fewest steps needed.

## Input

The first line is `n`, the number of cases. Each case is a line `x y` with `0 ≤ x ≤ y < 2³¹`.

## Output

For each case, print the minimum number of steps.

855.statement:
Friends live at street and avenue corners of a grid city, where walking one block costs one unit. Choose a meeting corner that minimises the total walking distance of everyone. If several corners tie, choose the one with the smallest street number, then the smallest avenue number.

## Input

The first line is `T`. Each test case starts with `S A F`: streets and avenues (each at most 1000) and the number of friends (`0 < F ≤ 50000`), followed by `F` lines `street avenue`.

## Output

For each test case, print `(Street: s, Avenue: a)`.

907.statement:
A trail has `N` campsites; you know the distance from the start to the first campsite, between consecutive campsites, and from the last campsite to the end. You must camp exactly `K` nights, always at a campsite, so the hike takes `K + 1` days. Plan the stops so that the longest single day of walking is as short as possible.

## Input

Several test cases until the end of input. Each starts with `N K` (`0 < N ≤ 600`, `0 ≤ K ≤ 300`), followed by `N + 1` distances, one per line.

## Output

For each test case, print the smallest possible longest day.

913.statement:
Joana writes the odd numbers in rows of growing odd length: `1`, then `3 5 7`, then `9 11 13 15 17`, and so on. Given the length `N` of a row, find the sum of the last three numbers in that row.

## Input

One odd number `N` per line (`1 < N < 10⁹`) until the end of input.

## Output

For each `N`, print the sum. It always fits in a signed 64 bit integer.

929.statement:
A grid of digits 0 to 9 is a maze; entering a cell costs its digit, including the starting cell. Moving is allowed up, down, left and right. Find the smallest total cost from the top left cell to the bottom right cell.

## Input

The first line is the number of mazes. Each maze gives the number of rows `N`, then the number of columns `M` (`1 ≤ N, M ≤ 999`), then `N` lines of `M` digits separated by spaces.

## Output

For each maze, print the minimum cost.

948.statement:
Every positive integer can be written uniquely as a sum of different Fibonacci numbers (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...) where no two consecutive Fibonacci numbers are used. Write that sum as a binary string: from right to left the positions stand for 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ..., and a `1` marks a number that is used. For example `17 = 13 + 3 + 1 = 100101`.

## Input

The first line is `N` (`1 ≤ N ≤ 500`), followed by `N` positive integers below 10⁸, one per line.

## Output

For each number `d`, print `d = s (fib)` where `s` is its representation without leading zeros.

967.statement:
A circular prime stays prime every time its first digit is moved to the end. For example 19937, 99371, 93719, 37199 and 71993 are all prime, so 19937 is a circular prime. Count the circular primes in a range.

## Input

One pair `i j` per line with `100 ≤ i ≤ j < 1000000`. A line with `-1` ends the input.

## Output

For each pair print `No Circular Primes.`, `1 Circular Prime.` or `n Circular Primes.`
967.sample_output:
No Circular Primes.
1 Circular Prime.
12 Circular Primes.

993.statement:
For a non negative integer `N`, find the smallest positive integer `Q` whose digits multiply to exactly `N`.

## Input

The first line is the number of data sets. Each next line holds one `N` with `0 ≤ N ≤ 10⁹`.

## Output

For each `N`, print `Q`, or `-1` if no such number exists.

1056.statement:
In a network of people with two way relationships, the separation of two people is the fewest relationships linking them. Find the largest separation over all pairs of people, or report that some pair is not connected at all.

## Input

Several networks. Each starts with `P R` (`2 ≤ P ≤ 50` people, `R ≥ 1` relationships), followed by `R` pairs of names, which may be spread over several lines. Names have no spaces. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For network `k`, print `Network k: d` with the largest separation, or `Network k: DISCONNECTED`, then an empty line.

## Notes

Some of the `P` people may not appear in any relationship.

1062.statement:
Containers arrive one by one, each labeled with the letter of the ship it belongs to. Each new container goes on top of an existing stack or starts a new one. Afterwards the ships are loaded in alphabetical order, and a ship can only take containers from the tops of stacks. Find the fewest stacks that make this possible.

## Input

One test case per line: 1 to 1000 uppercase letters in arrival order. A line with `end` ends the input.

## Output

For test case `k`, print `Case k: s`.

1101.title: To Add or to Multiply
1101.statement:
A processor knows two instructions: `A` adds `a` and `M` multiplies by `m`. Every input lies between `p` and `q`, and every output must lie between `r` and `s`. Find the shortest program that works for all inputs in the range; if several have the same length, choose the first in lexicographic order of `A` and `M`.

## Input

One case per line: `a m p q r s`, all between 1 and 10⁹, with `p ≤ q` and `r ≤ s`. Six zeros end the input.

## Output

For case `k` print `Case k: ` followed by the program written as alternating groups like `1A 2M`, or `empty` if no instruction is needed, or `impossible` if no program works.
1101.sample_output:
Case 1: 1A 2M
Case 2: 1M 2A 1M
Case 3: impossible
Case 4: empty

1200.statement:
Solve a linear equation in one variable `x`. Each side is a sum of terms joined by `+` or `-`; a term is an integer, an integer followed by `x`, or just `x` (meaning `1x`). There are no unary signs and no spaces.

## Input

The first line is `t` (`1 ≤ t ≤ 10`), followed by `t` equations, each at most 255 characters. Coefficients are between 0 and 1000.

## Output

For each equation, print the floor of the solution (the largest integer not above it), `IMPOSSIBLE` if there is no solution, or `IDENTITY` if every `x` is a solution.

1208.statement:
Cities named `A`, `B`, `C`, ... are joined by tunnels, and protecting each tunnel needs some number of guards. Choose tunnels to protect so that all cities stay connected through protected tunnels, using the fewest guards in total.

## Input

The first line is the number of test cases. Each case starts with the number of cities `n`, followed by an `n × n` matrix with values separated by commas and spaces: entry `(i, j)` is the guards needed for the tunnel between city `i` and city `j`, or 0 if there is no tunnel.

## Output

For test case `k` print `Case k:`, then each chosen tunnel as `X-Y w`, with the earlier letter first, in increasing order of `w` and alphabetically for equal `w`.
1208.sample_output:
Case 1:
B-D 3
D-F 4
E-F 5
C-E 6
A-F 7

1225.statement:
Write all integers from 1 to `N` one after another and count how often each digit 0 to 9 appears.

## Input

The first line is the number of data sets (at most 20). Each next line holds one `N` with `1 < N < 10000`.

## Output

For each `N`, print the ten counts for digits 0 to 9 on one line, separated by spaces.

1234.statement:
A connected road network has junctions and two way roads, and putting a camera on a road has a cost. A circuit is any route of three or more roads that returns to its start without reusing a road. Choose roads for cameras so that every possible circuit has at least one camera, at the smallest total cost.

## Input

The first line is the number of data sets `c`. Each data set starts with `n m` (`0 < n < 10000` junctions, `0 < m < 100000` roads), followed by `m` lines `a b cost` (cost 1 to 1000). A line with `0` follows the last data set.

## Output

For each data set, print the minimum total cost.

1237.statement:
A database lists car makers, each with the lowest and highest price of any car they made. For each queried price, find the maker whose range contains it. If no maker or more than one maker matches, the answer is undetermined.

## Input

The first line is `T` (`T ≤ 10`). Each case gives `D` (`D < 10000`), then `D` lines `name L H` (`0 < L < H < 1000000`, names without spaces), then `Q` (`Q < 1000`), then `Q` prices, one per line. Ranges include both ends.

## Output

For each query, print the maker's name or `UNDETERMINED`. Put an empty line between cases.

1260.statement:
For each day after the first, count how many earlier days had sales less than or equal to that day's sales. Print the total of these counts.

## Input

The first line is `T`. Each case has a line with `n` (`2 ≤ n ≤ 1000`) and a line with `n` sales values between 1 and 5000.

## Output

For each case, print the total.

1316.statement:
Each product brings a profit if it is sold by its deadline. Selling a product takes exactly one time unit, one product at a time, starting at time 0; a product with deadline `d` must finish by time `d`. Choose which products to sell and in what order to make the most profit.

## Input

Product sets until the end of input. Each set is `n` (`0 ≤ n ≤ 10000`) followed by `n` pairs `profit deadline`, each value between 1 and 10000. Whitespace, including line breaks, can appear anywhere.

## Output

For each set, print the best total profit on its own line.

1339.statement:
A message was encrypted in two steps: first every letter was replaced by another letter (different letters always map to different letters), then the letters were shuffled into a new order. Given an encrypted message and a candidate original of the same length, decide whether the candidate could have produced it.

## Input

Pairs of lines until the end of input: the encrypted message, then the candidate original. Both use only uppercase letters and have the same length, at most 100.

## Output

For each pair, print `YES` or `NO`.

HEHE
AAA
AAA

SECRETMESSAGES

1366.statement:
A grid of `n` rows and `m` columns holds two minerals; each cell has an amount of each. One refinery is to the west and one is to the north. In each cell you build at most one conveyor: a westward belt for the first mineral or a northward belt for the second. A cell's mineral only counts if it rides an unbroken straight line of belts of the right type all the way to its refinery. Maximise the total mineral delivered.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with `n m` (`1 ≤ n, m ≤ 500`). The next `n` lines give the first mineral and the following `n` lines the second, row by row from north to south, each row from west to east, with values from 0 to 1000. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each test case, print the maximum total.

1368.statement:
Given `m` DNA strings of length `n`, find a string `y` of length `n` that minimises the total Hamming distance to all of them (the number of positions where `y` and each string differ, summed over all strings). If several strings tie, choose the smallest in alphabetical order.

## Input

The first line is `T`. Each case starts with `m n` (`4 ≤ m ≤ 50`, `4 ≤ n ≤ 1000`), followed by `m` strings over `A`, `C`, `G`, `T`.

## Output

For each case, print the chosen string on one line and its total distance on the next.

1513.statement:
A stack holds movies 1 to `n` with movie 1 on top. To watch a movie, it is taken out of the stack and afterwards put back on top. For every request, report how many movies were above the requested one just before it was taken out.

## Input

The first line is the number of test cases (at most 100). Each case has a line `n m` (`1 ≤ n, m ≤ 100000`) and a line with the `m` requested movie numbers.

## Output

For each case, print the `m` answers on one line, separated by spaces.

1583.statement:
The digit sum of `N` here means `N` plus the sum of its digits; for example 245 gives 245 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 256, so 245 is a generator of 256. Find the smallest generator of a given number.

## Input

The first line is `T`. Each next line holds one `N` with `1 ≤ N ≤ 100000`.

## Output

For each `N`, print its smallest generator, or `0` if it has none.

1585.statement:
A test result is a string of `O` (correct) and `X` (wrong). A correct answer scores the length of the run of consecutive `O`s ending at it, so `OOO` scores 1 + 2 + 3; a wrong answer scores 0. Find the total score.

## Input

The first line is `T`. Each next line holds one string of `O` and `X`, with length between 1 and 79.

## Output

For each string, print the total score.

1587.statement:
Six rectangular boards are given by their width and height. Decide whether they can be the six faces of a box, using each board for one face. Boards may be turned.

## Input

Test cases until the end of input, six lines each, every line holding `w h` (1 to 10000).

## Output

For each test case, print `POSSIBLE` or `IMPOSSIBLE`.

1594.statement:
From a tuple `(a1, ..., an)`, the next tuple is `(|a1 - a2|, |a2 - a3|, ..., |an - a1|)`. Repeating this either reaches all zeros or falls into a repeating loop. Decide which happens.

## Input

The first line is `T`. Each case has a line with `n` (`3 ≤ n ≤ 15`) and a line with `n` integers from 0 to 1000. Either outcome shows up within 1000 steps.

## Output

For each case, print `ZERO` or `LOOP`.

1632.statement:
Treasures lie at different points of a straight road, each with a deadline after which it vanishes. You start at any point you like at time 0, walk one unit of distance per time unit, and pick up a treasure instantly when you reach it. Collect all treasures before their deadlines, finishing as early as possible.

## Input

Data sets until the end of input. Each is `n` (`n ≤ 10000`) followed by `n` pairs `position deadline`, in increasing order of position. Whitespace can appear anywhere.

## Output

For each data set, print the earliest time all treasures can be collected, or `No solution`.

1640.statement:
Write down every integer between `a` and `b`, inclusive, and count how many times each digit 0 to 9 appears.

## Input

Up to 500 lines with `a b`, both between 1 and 10⁸ exclusive. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each line, print the ten counts for digits 0 to 9, separated by single spaces.

## Notes

`a` can be larger than `b`.

1644.statement:
Between two consecutive primes `p` and `p + n` lie `n - 1` composite numbers; they form a prime gap of length `n`. For a given number `k`, print the length of the prime gap containing it, or 0 if `k` is prime.

## Input

One integer per line, greater than 1 and at most 1299709. A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each number, print the gap length or 0.

1650.statement:
The signature of a permutation of 1 to `n` is the string of `n - 1` letters where each letter is `I` if the next element is larger and `D` if it is smaller. For example `3 1 2 7 4 6 5` has signature `DIIDID`. Given a signature in which some letters may be `?` (either `I` or `D`), count the permutations that match.

## Input

One signature per line until the end of input, 1 to 1000 characters from `I`, `D` and `?`.

## Output

For each signature, print the count modulo `1000000007`.

1657.statement:
A game master picks two different integers `X` and `Y` from 1 to `N`, tells their sum to player S and their product to player P. Both players know `N`, think perfectly and know the other does too. Taking turns, S first, each says either that they do not know the pair yet or that they now know it.

Given `N` and the number `M` of times "I don't know" was said in total before a player finally knew the numbers, list every pair that could have been chosen.

## Input

Data sets until the end of input, each a line `N M` (`2 ≤ N ≤ 200`, `0 ≤ M ≤ 100`).

## Output

For each data set, print the number of possible pairs, then each pair as `x y` with `x < y`, one per line. Pairs may be printed in any order.

1714.statement:
A virtual keyboard is a grid; each key covers one or more connected cells. The cursor starts at the top left cell. The four arrows move it to the next cell in that direction belonging to a different key (it stays put if there is none), and a fifth button types the key under the cursor. Each button press is one stroke. Find the fewest strokes to type a text and then the Enter key `*`.

## Input

Test cases until the end of input. Each gives `r c` (`1 ≤ r, c ≤ 50`), then `r` lines of `c` characters (uppercase letters, digits, `-`, and `*` for Enter), then the text to type: up to 10000 available characters other than `*`.

## Output

For each test case, print the minimum number of strokes, including the final Enter.

1730.statement:
For a number `N`, consider all sets of distinct positive integers whose least common multiple is exactly `N`. `MSLCM(N)` is the largest possible sum of such a set. Given `N`, compute `MSLCM(2) + MSLCM(3) + ... + MSLCM(N)`.

## Input

Up to 200 lines, each with `N` (`1 < N ≤ 20000000`). A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each `N`, print the sum.

## Notes

The answer does not fit in a 32 bit integer.

1746.statement:
A 1-quotation is a quote character, some non quote text, and a quote character. For `k > 1`, a k-quotation is `k` quote characters, then a non empty sequence of (k-1)-quotations with optional non quote text around and between them, then `k` quote characters.

A string is given only as the lengths of its blocks of consecutive quote characters, with non quote text between consecutive blocks. Find the largest `k` for which it is a k-quotation.

## Input

Test cases until the end of input. Each is a line with `n` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 100`) and a line with `n` block lengths (1 to 100).

## Output

For each test case, print the largest `k`, or `no quotation`.

10004.statement:
Decide whether the nodes of a connected undirected graph can be colored with two colors so that every edge joins nodes of different colors.

## Input

Several test cases. Each gives `n` (`1 < n < 200`) on one line, the number of edges on the next, then one edge per line as two node numbers from 0 to `n - 1`. `n = 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each graph, print `BICOLORABLE.` or `NOT BICOLORABLE.`

10010.statement:
Find words in a grid of letters. A word may run in any of the eight directions (horizontal, vertical or diagonal, forwards or backwards) and letter case is ignored. For each word, report where its first letter is.

## Input

The first line is the number of cases, then an empty line. Each case gives `m n` (`1 ≤ m, n ≤ 50`), then `m` lines of `n` letters, then `k` (`1 ≤ k ≤ 20`), then `k` words. Cases are separated by empty lines. Every word appears at least once.

## Output

For each word print `row column` (1 based) of its first letter. If it appears several times, use the occurrence whose first letter is highest, and among those the leftmost. Put an empty line between cases.

10018.statement:
Repeatedly add a number to its digit reversal until the result is a palindrome. For example 195 gives 786, 1473, 5214 and then 9339 after four additions.

## Input

The first line is `N` (`0 < N ≤ 100`), followed by `N` numbers. Every case reaches a palindrome in fewer than 1000 additions, and the palindrome is at most 4294967295.

## Output

For each number, print the number of additions and the palindrome, separated by a space.

## Notes

At least one addition is always performed, even if the starting number is already a palindrome.

10025.statement:
Put `+` or `-` in front of each of `1, 2, ..., n` so that the total equals `k`. For example `-1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 - 7 = 12`. Find the smallest `n` for which this is possible.

## Input

The first line is the number of test cases, then an empty line. Each test case is one integer `k` with `|k| ≤ 10⁹`, and test cases are separated by empty lines.

## Output

For each `k`, print the smallest `n` (at least 1). Put an empty line between consecutive outputs.

10026.statement:
A shoemaker has `N` jobs and works on one at a time. Job `i` takes `T` days, and for every day before work on it starts he pays a fine of `S` cents. Find the order of jobs with the smallest total fine; if several orders are best, give the lexicographically smallest list of job numbers.

## Input

The first line is the number of cases, then an empty line. Each case gives `N` (`1 ≤ N ≤ 1000`), then `N` lines `T S` (`1 ≤ T ≤ 1000`, `1 ≤ S ≤ 10000`). Cases are separated by empty lines.

## Output

For each case, print the job numbers (1 based) in order on one line, separated by spaces. Put an empty line between cases.

10032.statement:
Split `n` people into two teams whose sizes differ by at most one, so that the total weights of the teams are as close as possible.

## Input

The first line is the number of cases, then an empty line. Each case gives `n` (at most 100), then `n` weights, one per line, each between 1 and 450. Cases are separated by empty lines.

## Output

For each case, print the two team weights, smaller first. Put an empty line between cases.

10035.statement:
Count how many carries happen when two numbers are added digit by digit from the right, the way it is taught in school.

## Input

Pairs of non negative integers with fewer than 10 digits, one pair per line. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each pair print `No carry operation.`, `1 carry operation.` or `n carry operations.`
10035.sample_output:
No carry operation.
3 carry operations.
1 carry operation.

10038.statement:
A sequence of `n` integers is jolly if the absolute differences between neighbours include every value from 1 to `n - 1`. A single number is always jolly.

## Input

One sequence per line until the end of input: `n` (`n ≤ 3000`) followed by the `n` integers.

## Output

For each sequence, print `Jolly` or `Not jolly`.

10050.statement:
Each political party calls a strike every `h` days: on days `h`, `2h`, `3h`, and so on. Day 1 is a Sunday, and Fridays and Saturdays are holidays on which nobody strikes. Count the working days lost to strikes in the first `N` days; a day with several strikes counts once.

## Input

The first line is `T`. Each case gives `N` (`7 ≤ N ≤ 3650`), then `P` (`1 ≤ P ≤ 100`), then `P` values `h`, one per line, none a multiple of 7.

## Output

For each case, print the number of lost working days.

10056.statement:
`N` players take turns, player 1 first, then 2, up to `N`, then player 1 again. On each throw the thrower wins with probability `p`, and the game ends at the first win. Find the probability that player `I` wins.

## Input

The first line is `S` (`S ≤ 1000`). Each next line holds `N p I` with `N ≤ 1000` and `1 ≤ I ≤ N`.

## Output

For each line, print the probability with four digits after the decimal point.

## Notes

`p` can be 0.

10066.statement:
Two towers are stacks of round tiles, listed by radius from top to bottom. Remove tiles from both so that the two remaining towers are identical, keeping the tiles in their original order. Find the largest number of tiles each remaining tower can have.

## Input

Several blocks. Each has `N1 N2` (`1 ≤ N1, N2 ≤ 100`), then a line with the `N1` radii of the first tower and a line with the `N2` radii of the second. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For block `k`, print `Twin Towers #k`, then `Number of Tiles : t`, then an empty line.
10066.sample_output:
Twin Towers #1
Number of Tiles : 4

Twin Towers #2
Number of Tiles : 6

10071.statement:
A particle starts with some velocity and moves with constant acceleration. After time `t` its velocity is `v`. Find how far it has moved after time `2t`.

## Input

One pair `v t` per line until the end of input, with `-100 ≤ v ≤ 100` and `0 ≤ t ≤ 200`.

## Output

For each pair, print the displacement as an integer.

10074.statement:
A map of a forest is a grid of `1` (a tree) and `0` (no tree). Find the largest rectangle of cells that contains no tree, measured by its number of cells.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with `M N` (`1 ≤ M, N ≤ 100`), followed by `M` lines of `N` symbols separated by single spaces. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For each test case, print the largest area.

10082.statement:
Text was typed with both hands placed one key too far to the right on a QWERTY keyboard, so every key pressed is the right neighbour of the intended one. Decode the text by replacing each character with the key immediately to its left.

## Input

Lines of text until the end of input, made of digits, spaces, uppercase letters (never `Q`, `A` or `Z`) and the punctuation keys of a standard keyboard (never the back quote).

## Output

Print each decoded line. Spaces stay as they are.

10099.statement:
A guide must take `T` tourists from city `S` to city `D`. Every road has a bus with a passenger limit. The guide picks one route and repeats it as often as needed; the guide travels on every trip and takes one seat. Find the fewest trips needed.

## Input

Several test cases. Each starts with `N R` (`N ≤ 100` cities), then `R` lines `C1 C2 P` (a two way road whose bus carries `P > 1` people, the guide included), then a line `S D T`. `0 0` ends the input.

## Output

For test case `k`, print `Scenario #k`, then `Minimum Number of Trips = x`, then an empty line.

10101.statement:
Write a number in words using Bangla units: `kuti` (10⁷), `lakh` (10⁵), `hajar` (10³) and `shata` (100). Parts larger than a kuti are themselves written with the same units. For example 45897458973958 becomes `45 lakh 89 hajar 7 shata 45 kuti 89 lakh 73 hajar 9 shata 58`. Units whose part is 0 are left out.

## Input

One non negative number per line, at most 999999999999999, until the end of input.

## Output

For case `k`, print `k` right aligned in 4 characters, a period, then the text, separated by single spaces as in the sample.
10101.sample_output:
1. 23 hajar 7 shata 64
   2. 45 lakh 89 hajar 7 shata 45 kuti 89 lakh 73 hajar 9 shata 58

10106.statement:
Multiply two non negative integers that can have up to 250 digits each.

## Input

Pairs of lines until the end of input, one number per line.

## Output

For each pair, print the exact product.

10125.statement:
In a set `S` of distinct integers, find the largest `d` such that `a + b + c = d` for some `a`, `b`, `c` and `d` that are four different elements of `S`.

## Input

Several sets. Each starts with `n` (`1 ≤ n ≤ 1000`), followed by the `n` elements, one per line, each between -536870912 and 536870911. A line with `0` ends the input.

## Output

For each set, print `d`, or `no solution`.

10130.statement:
A family visits a sale where each person may take at most one item of each kind. Every item has a price and a weight, and every person can carry a maximum weight. Find the largest total price of items the family can carry home.

## Input

The first line is `T`. Each case gives `N` (`1 ≤ N ≤ 1000`), then `N` lines `P W` (price 1 to 100, weight 1 to 30), then `G` (`1 ≤ G ≤ 100`), then `G` lines with each person's limit (1 to 30).

## Output

10190.statement:

`n` and `m` can be 0 or 1.

10200.statement:
Euler's formula `n² + n + 41` is prime for every `n` from 0 to 39 but not always after that. For a range `a ≤ n ≤ b`, find what percentage of the values it produces are prime.

Pairs `a b` with `0 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ 10000`, one per line, until the end of input.

## Output

For each pair, print the percentage rounded to two decimal places.

10221.statement:

One case per line until the end of input: `s a unit`, where `unit` is `deg` or `min`.

For each case, print the arc distance and the straight line distance in km, separated by a space, each with six digits after the decimal point.

10222.statement:
A professor's text was typed with every key two places to the right of the intended one on a standard keyboard. Decode it by replacing each letter or punctuation key with the key two places to its left. Spaces stay as they are.

For each case, print the `x y` coordinates of the fourth corner with three digits after the decimal point.

10268.statement:
Evaluate the derivative of a polynomial `a0·xⁿ + a1·xⁿ⁻¹ + ... + an` at a given `x`.

Pairs of lines until the end of input: a line with `x`, then a line with the coefficients `a0 a1 ... an`. All values and results fit in a 32 bit signed integer.

10273.statement:
Each cow repeats a milk pattern: cow `i` has a cycle of `T` days with given amounts. For each case, print the number of cows never eaten and the day of the last meal, or 0 if no cow is eaten.

10326.statement:
Build the polynomial equation with leading coefficient 1 whose roots are exactly the given integers, and print it.

Cases until the end of input. Each is a line with `N` (`N ≤ 50`) and a line with the `N` integer roots. No coefficient exceeds 10¹⁵.

10327.statement:

Given a set of sticks, decide whether all of them can be joined end to end to form the four sides of a square. Every stick must be used, and sticks cannot be broken.

For each test case, print `yes` or `no`.
